A favorite optimistic view of the future of AI is from a pessimistic book that not about AI: "Rise and Fall of American Growth," which argues that we had a one-time explosion in living standards from 1870 and 1920 (& later outside the US). In 1870: no toilets, no city plumbing, lamp light, no central heating, little public health, horses for local travel, etc. In 50 years, all of this was solved & the nation was electrified. In the next fifty modern medicine, air travel and telecommunication happened. The book then points out that we have had no changes in lifestyle of similar scale since the 1970s. Written in 2016, it argued that we would likely never experience another boom like the "Special Century." The positive view of AI should make us ask "But what if we do?" and "How do we make it all go right?"

It isn't that weird to think that "this time is different" - we had a couple of Industrial Revolutions over the past couple centuries, just because we got used to a relatively steady-state regime post World War Two with a regular pace of growth doesn't mean it continues forever. Across our projects @GoogleDeepMind, we are witnessing a genuine phase transition in the pace of scientific discovery. You will see a glimpse of this in our releases in the next few weeks.

Must-read paper on scaling multi-agent swarms. The main focus right now is training agent swarms to coordinate and cooperate better. Here is a promising new work on this. The problem: Multi-agent systems usually follow a plan that a developer writes ahead of time. The plan decides which agent does what and when agents message each other, and it usually stays the same across tasks. What they propose: s3 has the agents learn that plan instead. Agents learn through cooperative RL when to work alone, when to share findings, and when to read teammates' work. There are no predefined roles. With matched training and inference budgets, s3 swarms tested at twice their training size solve over 25x more coordination problems than the strongest baseline. In parallel exploration, communicating agents repeat nearly 50% less work and beat best-of-N by up to 9.4 points. The agents develop complementary roles on their own, and those roles carry over to bigger teams. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08615 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/s-3-simple-scaling-of-swarms-via-cooperative-multi-agent-rl-2611.08615

Banger paper from Google on quantum AI. They gave teams of LLM agents the ability to write quantum programs and prove them correct in Lean. Classical computers can only test quantum algorithms on small instances. A simulation-scored search loop can't reach the sizes where quantum computing becomes useful. So researchers write a specification and a cost target as a Lean theorem. Agent teams propose programs, the Lean kernel checks correctness and cost, and a separate comparator re-verifies every accepted answer. Teams share results and dead ends on a wiki and meet at scheduled conferences to exchange ideas. The verified programs cut the cost of quantum arithmetic by 290x against the best prior baseline. Simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry, and drug metabolism improved by 11x, 8x, and 2.5x. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09822 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/discovering-formally-verified-quantum-programs-with-ai-2611.09822

What do you teach computer science students when an agent can one-shot all of their homework? I sat down with @swyx on @latentspacepod to walk through how I'm answering that in my Stanford course 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗦𝗼𝗳𝘁𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿, and how the same ideas show up day to day at @MonacoGTM. Last year all students were just using tab complete. This year when I surveyed them, every one was regularly using autonomous agents. Exercises that once taught the workflow were starting to feel one-shotable. So the curriculum shifted toward judgment: 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀: students write a small coding agent from scratch (about 200 lines), then intercept the harness of a state of the art coding agent and read the system, plan, and compaction prompts. To effectively use and build agents you need to understand the loop they run in. 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀: part of the homework is contributing to open-source projects. Maintainers review the patch and help students build mental models of good software. An agent can draft the change but getting it accepted still requires appropriate context, architecture, and intent within a complex codebase 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲: before implementation, research an unfamiliar repo, propose a few approaches, and choose one. After the agent writes code, quiz yourself on the diff until you can defend it without reopening the file. At Monaco, that judgment is most of the job. When agents can build almost anything, the hard call is what's worth building. We buy tools to learn a space, then build only the pieces that have to fit our own infrastructure. Code review has stayed a bought product for a while (though that's starting to change!). Agent workspaces, where background agents run the app and test patches, we built ourselves. Great work on harness self-improvement from Microsoft and colleagues. It discusses how to build long-running agents that improve their own harness, It turns out that if you run agents for hours, giving them a way to fix their own harness during the run improves results on long-running problems. More from the paper: Harness optimization usually runs offline. You tune the harness on tasks that have reference answers, then reuse it. Long open-ended tasks have no reference answers, and they run into problems the tuned harness never saw. BOXBOX moves that loop into the task itself. The agent decides when to revise its harness, and a kernel hot-reloads the new version while keeping the full execution context, so the run continues without a restart. They test it on PerfRace, a new benchmark where agents spend hours speeding up real software projects. Under the same time and cost budget, BOXBOX reaches a 1.70x speedup at four hours, against 1.54x for the best baseline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09218 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/boxbox-recursive-harness-self-improvement-for-long-running-performance-optimizat-2611.09218
